data.name: Cutting_Lead
data.value: A cutting is a piece of stem that grows its own roots and becomes a new plant. Most climbing and trailing houseplants, like pothos, philodendron and tradescantia, root easily this way.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Cutting_WhenTitle
data.value: When
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: heading.

data.name: Cutting_When
data.value: Cuttings root fastest in late spring and early summer, while the plant is growing, but they root at most times of year. Many growers find rooting slower in a cool room.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: when to take one.

data.name: Cutting_Need
data.value: Clean, sharp scissors or a knife, and a glass, pot or box for what it roots in.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: what to have ready.

data.name: Cutting_Step1
data.value: Pick a healthy stem the plant can spare, with no pests on it.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 1.

data.name: Cutting_Step2
data.value: Find the nodes: the joints where a leaf meets the stem, often with a bump or a small brown root. Roots grow from the nodes.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 2.

data.name: Cutting_Step3
data.value: Cut just below a node, so the piece is about 8 to 10 cm long with two or more nodes. A tip cutting usually roots fastest.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 3.

data.name: Cutting_Step4
data.value: Take off the lower leaves and any flowers, and keep 2 or 3 leaves at the top. Leaves that would sit in water or compost rot there.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 4.

data.name: Cutting_Step5
data.value: For succulents, cacti, pelargoniums and rubber plants, leave the cut end to dry and seal for a day or so first.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 5.

data.name: Cutting_Step6
data.value: Rooting powder is optional. Some sources dip the end in it, others don't use it, and easy plants like pothos root well without.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: step 6.

data.name: Cutting_RootIn
data.value: Root it in
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: label over the choice of what to root in.

data.name: Cutting_Water
data.value: Water
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_Mix
data.value: Cutting mix
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_Sphagnum
data.value: Sphagnum moss
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: name of a method.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWhy
data.value: You can see the roots come, and it needs nothing but a glass. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_WaterSteps
data.value: Stand the cutting in water with a node under the surface and the leaves above it. Keep it in a bright spot out of direct sun. Change the water every few days so it stays clean.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: steps.

data.name: Cutting_WaterHowLong
data.value: About 10 days for the easiest, 3 to 4 weeks for most.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: how long.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWinter
data.value: In winter, when cuttings root slowly, they may rot in water before they root, and a mix does better.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: a note about winter.

data.name: Cutting_WaterWatch
data.value: Cloudy or smelly water and a soft brown stem end mean rot. Many growers cut above it and start again in fresh water. Roots grown in water are used to water, so the move to compost is the risky part. See Potting it up.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, water: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_MixWhy
data.value: The roots grow in what the plant will live in, so there is no move from water to compost. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_MixSteps
data.value: Fill a small pot with half peat-free multipurpose compost and half perlite, or equal parts peat and perlite, vermiculite or sand. Make a hole with a pencil, set the cutting in so a node is buried and the leaves sit just above the surface, and water well.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: steps.

data.name: Cutting_MixKeep
data.value: Keep the mix moist but not soggy. A clear bag over the pot, or a clear box or jar, keeps the air around it damp. Keep it out of direct sun, which heats it up. Some growers open the cover now and then for air.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: keeping it damp.

data.name: Cutting_MixHowLong
data.value: 1 to 2 weeks for soft stems, about 3 to 4 weeks for most. Many growers read a gentle tug that meets resistance as roots.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: how long.

data.name: Cutting_MixWatch
data.value: Mould on the surface or a blackened stem, which many growers put down to too wet a mix or too little air.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, mix: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumWhy
data.value: It holds water and air at the same time, and many growers use it for aroids and hoyas.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: why people pick it.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumSteps
data.value: Wet the moss and put it in a clear cup, enough to cover the base of the cutting. Push the cutting gently in and cover the cup with plastic that doesn't touch the leaves. Keep it in bright light out of direct sun, and add water if the moss dries. Many growers squeeze the moss until it no longer drips.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: steps.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumHowLong
data.value: About a month.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: how long.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumGloves
data.value: Wear gloves: a rare skin infection has been linked to sphagnum moss, and a mask is advised when handling it dry.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: a safety note.

data.name: Cutting_SphagnumWatch
data.value: Moss kept dripping wet, which many growers say rots the stem.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting, sphagnum: what to watch for.

data.name: Cutting_PotTitle
data.value: Potting it up
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: heading.

data.name: Cutting_PotLead
data.value: Sources differ on how long to wait, and both ways are common:
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: line before the two ways to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotEarly
data.value: Early: pot it up once the roots are about 2.5 cm long, since short roots settle into compost more easily. Many growers say the same.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the early way to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotLater
data.value: Later: wait for a good set of roots and new growth before potting up.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: the later way to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_PotHow
data.value: Pot each one into a small pot, 8 to 10 cm, of peat-free multipurpose compost. Some growers keep the compost a little moister than usual for the first week or two while the roots get used to it. Others add a spoonful of compost to the water over a few days before the move.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: how to pot up.

data.name: Cutting_InApp
data.value: Mark the propagation Rooting when the first root shows and Rooted when it is ready, and Pot up when it goes into a pot. The days it took are then counted for you.
data.comment: Guide, taking a cutting: how it works in the app. Uses the names of the stages.

data.name: SemiHydro_Lead
data.value: In semi-hydro a plant grows in clay pebbles (LECA) or a mix of mineral grains like PON instead of soil, and drinks from water that stands at the bottom of the pot and that the pebbles soak up. The pebbles give off almost no nutrients, so the water carries the feed. The move from soil can be tricky, and rotting roots are the main risk.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: the lead paragraph.

data.name: SemiHydro_Where
data.value: No horticultural society or university has written about moving a houseplant from soil to semi-hydro. This guide is how growers and the makers of PON and hydroculture fertiliser describe it, and a line that only growers stand behind says so.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: why the sources are thin. Shown under the lead.

data.name: SemiHydro_WhichTitle
data.value: Which plants
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: heading.

data.name: SemiHydro_Which
data.value: Young plants and cuttings make the move most easily. An old plant that has grown in soil for years finds it harder. Robust plants like pothos, spider plant and peace lily are the easiest to start with. Some growers find that plants that like to dry out between waterings do less well with water always at their roots.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: which plants move best.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need1
data.value: LECA or PON.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need2
data.value: A pot with holes inside one without, or a self-watering pot, so the water stands below the roots. Many growers set it up this way.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need3
data.value: A fertiliser made for hydroculture, since the pebbles give off almost no nutrients.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Need4
data.value: An opaque pot, since light on the water grows algae, as many growers say.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: what to have ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_ReadyTitle
data.value: Get the medium ready
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: heading.

data.name: SemiHydro_Ready
data.value: Rinse LECA until the water runs clear, to wash off the clay dust. Many growers soak it for a few hours too. Some growers rinse PON, others use it straight from the bag.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: getting the pebbles ready.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step1
data.value: Take the plant out of its pot.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: step 1.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step2
data.value: Get all the soil off the roots. Many growers soak the root ball in a bowl of water first to loosen it, then work it loose with their fingers and rinse. Soil left between the pebbles packs down and rots, and some fine roots break off.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: step 2.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step3
data.value: Trim any soft, brown or rotten roots.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: step 3.

data.name: SemiHydro_Step4
data.value: Set the plant in the new pot and fill around the roots with the pebbles, at the depth it stood before, as many growers do.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: step 4.

data.name: SemiHydro_SetupTitle
data.value: Two ways to set up the pot
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: heading.

data.name: SemiHydro_Setup
data.value: The pot of pebbles can stand in the water, or stand above it with a wick drawing the water up. Many growers use each. The wick way has its own guide:
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: before the link to the wick guide.

data.name: SemiHydro_HowMove
data.value: How to move it
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: label over the choice of how to move.

data.name: SemiHydro_Straight
data.value: Straight in
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirst
data.value: Water roots first
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_Lechuza
data.value: Soil over PON (LECHUZA's way)
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: name of a method.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightWhy
data.value: One step, and the plant keeps its roots. Many growers pick it for that.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightHow
data.value: Move it straight into the pebbles after washing. Many growers keep the water low at first, just touching the bottom of the pebbles, and change it often.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_StraightWatch
data.value: Many growers see the old soil roots die back over the first weeks while new white water roots grow. Some leaves may yellow.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, straight in: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstWhy
data.value: The plant grows roots made for water before it goes into the pebbles, so less dies back, as many growers describe it.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstHow
data.value: After washing, stand the roots in water, change it every few days, and move the plant into the pebbles once new white roots have grown. Some growers use this mostly for small plants and cuttings.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_WaterFirstWatch
data.value: The same rot signs as in a glass: cloudy water and soft brown roots.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, water roots first: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaWhy
data.value: It is how LECHUZA, the maker of PON, tells you to start a plant in its planters.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: why people pick it.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaHow
data.value: LECHUZA's planters hold a layer of PON under potting soil, and the plant is set in the soil. For the first 3 months it is watered from above while the roots grow down, and only then does it drink from the reservoir. This is not a move to PON alone.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: how.

data.name: SemiHydro_LechuzaWatch
data.value: LECHUZA says to refill the reservoir only once its indicator reads min, after a dry phase of about 1 week for small plants and 2 for larger ones.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro, soil over PON: what to watch for.

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelTitle
data.value: The water level
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: heading.

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelLead
data.value: Growers keep it at different heights, and all of these are common:
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: line before the water levels.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level1
data.value: About a third of the pot's height, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level2
data.value: Just touching the bottom of the pebbles, so they wick the water up, say some growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_Level3
data.value: Some growers let the reservoir run empty for a few days before filling it again, so the roots get air. LECHUZA's instructions do the same, with a dry phase of about 1 to 2 weeks before each refill. Others keep it topped up all the time.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_LevelNever
data.value: The water shouldn't reach where the stem meets the roots, and the plant shouldn't stand in water all the time, as COMPO says too.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: a limit on the water level.

data.name: SemiHydro_SettlesTitle
data.value: While it settles
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: heading.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle1
data.value: Change the water and flush the pebbles with fresh water, rather than only topping up, so the roots get oxygen and salts don't build up. Once new roots are growing, COMPO and many growers do it every week or two.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle2
data.value: Feed: COMPO, a maker of hydroculture fertiliser, says a weak feed each week while the plant is growing. Some growers start straight away, others wait until new roots show.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle3
data.value: It takes weeks to months before new roots and a new leaf show, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_Settle4
data.value: Watch for: a sour smell, soft brown roots, or a white crust of salts on the pebbles, as many growers put it.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: while it settles.

data.name: SemiHydro_InApp
data.value: Moving to semi-hydro is in the More menu on a plant's page. The tracking card then asks for Roots washed, First new water root and First new leaf, and Today asks for a look if nothing happens for a while.
data.comment: Guide, moving to semi-hydro: how it works in the app. Uses the names of the tracking steps.

data.name: Wick_Lead
data.value: In a wick pot the plant's pot stands above a reservoir of water, and a cord runs from the water up into the mix. The water climbs the cord the way it climbs a strip of kitchen paper, and the mix takes up what it can hold. It works with soil and with semi-hydro, and many growers use it to water less often or while they are away.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Wick_WetTitle
data.value: How wet it gets
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Wet
data.value: The wick can't make the mix wetter than the mix itself holds. A mix that holds a lot of water stays too wet in a wick pot, which is why the mix matters more than the wick. A thicker wick only brings the water faster, so a big pot needs a thicker wick or more than one.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: how wet the mix gets.

data.name: Wick_Need1
data.value: A pot with a hole in the bottom, and a container for the water that the pot can stand on or in without touching the water. Some self-watering pots come with both.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: what to have ready.

data.name: Wick_Need2
data.value: A wick of synthetic cord, like nylon or acrylic yarn, or a strip of nylon stocking. Cotton and wool rot in the wet, and many growers avoid them.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: what to have ready.

data.name: Wick_Step1
data.value: Thread the wick through the hole in the bottom of the pot, so a few centimetres lie along the bottom inside and the rest hangs below.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 1.

data.name: Wick_Step2
data.value: Many growers wet the wick through before they start, so the water starts climbing at once.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 2.

data.name: Wick_Step3
data.value: Fill the pot with the mix and the plant, with the wick lying at the bottom. A wick pushed up into the middle makes the middle wetter.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 3.

data.name: Wick_Step4
data.value: Fill the container with water and stand the pot over it, so the wick hangs in the water but the bottom of the pot never touches it.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 4.

data.name: Wick_Step5
data.value: Many growers water once from the top to settle the mix around the roots.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: step 5.

data.name: Wick_GrowsIn
data.value: What it grows in
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: label over the choice of what it grows in.

data.name: Wick_Soil
data.value: Soil
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: name of a method.

data.name: Wick_SemiHydro
data.value: Semi-hydro
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: name of a method.

data.name: Wick_SoilWhy
data.value: The plant stays in soil and simply gets its water from below.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: why people pick it.

data.name: Wick_SoilMix
data.value: An ordinary potting mix stays too wet. Wick growers open it up with a lot of perlite, often half the mix or more.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: the mix.

data.name: Wick_SoilWatch
data.value: The top of the mix staying dry on a plant with few roots. Water small plants and new cuttings from the top for a few weeks until the roots reach down.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, soil: what to watch for.

data.name: Wick_SemiWhy
data.value: The pebbles never stand in the water, so the roots always have air, and a slow drinker is less likely to rot, as many growers see it.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: why people pick it.

data.name: Wick_SemiMix
data.value: LECA alone wicks poorly, since the round pebbles barely touch. Many growers use PON, pumice or perlite, or mix some into the LECA.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: the mix.

data.name: Wick_SemiWatch
data.value: A dry top layer. Roots that grow out through the hole into the water are fine, say many growers.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick, semi-hydro: what to watch for.

data.name: Wick_CareTitle
data.value: Looking after it
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Care1
data.value: Fill the container before it runs dry. A dry wick stops drawing and has to be wetted again.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care2
data.value: Liquid feed can go in the water. Many growers use it weaker than on the bottle, since it goes in every time.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care3
data.value: Water from the top now and then, which flushes out salts that build up when water only comes from below. Many growers do.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care4
data.value: Keep light off the water, or it grows algae. The colour of the wick doesn't matter.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_Care5
data.value: Many growers change the wick if it goes slimy or stops drawing.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: looking after it.

data.name: Wick_DisagreeTitle
data.value: Where growers disagree
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: heading.

data.name: Wick_Disagree1
data.value: Wick or no wick in semi-hydro: some growers wick every pot, others take the wicks out and let the pebbles stand in a shallow layer of water instead.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: where growers disagree.

data.name: Wick_Disagree2
data.value: How thick: some growers split a yarn into single strands for small pots. One careful source says thickness only changes how fast the water comes, not how wet the mix is.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: where growers disagree.

data.name: Wick_InApp
data.value: A pot can be marked as a self-watering pot with a wick on the Pots page, and the watering reminder then learns how long the water lasts instead of how long the soil takes to dry.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: how it works in the app.

data.name: Wick_Where
data.value: No RHS or extension page covers wick pots for houseplants beyond a mention in one old Cornell paper. The most careful page found leans on research for how wet a mix stays, one source is a pot maker, and the rest is what growers do.
data.comment: Guide, watering through a wick: why the sources are thin. Shown under the lead.

data.name: Mix_Lead
data.value: A potting mix is a base that holds water with something added for air. Roots need both, and how much of each depends on the plant. Compost also breaks down and packs tighter over time, which is why plants are moved into fresh mix every couple of years.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: the lead paragraph.

data.name: Mix_Water
data.value: Many growers match the mix to how they water: a mix that drains fast suits someone who waters often, and one that holds more suits someone who waters less often.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: matching the mix to how you water.

data.name: Mix_InTitle
data.value: What goes in
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: heading over the list of ingredients.

data.name: Mix_Garden
data.value: Garden soil can go in a mix, but it may carry pests, disease and weed seeds unless it is sterilised first.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a note on garden soil.

data.name: Mix_InMultipurpose
data.value: Peat-free multipurpose compost
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InMultipurposeDoes
data.value: The usual base.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InPeat
data.value: Peat
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InPeatDoes
data.value: Holds a lot of water and is acidic. Many people avoid it, since digging it harms peat bogs, and the RHS stopped selling it in 2019.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InCoir
data.value: Coir
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InCoirDoes
data.value: Coconut husk, used instead of peat. Holds water but lets the rest drain, and is close to neutral.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InLoam
data.value: Loam-based compost (John Innes No 2 in the UK)
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InLoamDoes
data.value: Heavier, so tall plants don't tip over.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InBark
data.value: Bark
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InBarkDoes
data.value: Air and drainage. The base for orchids. Use bark that has been aged.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InPerlite
data.value: Perlite
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InPerliteDoes
data.value: Light white grains that add air and drainage.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InPumice
data.value: Pumice
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InPumiceDoes
data.value: Adds air and holds a little water. Good for thick roots.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InGrit
data.value: Grit or coarse sand
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InGritDoes
data.value: Drainage and weight. Fine sand makes the mix dense.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InVermiculite
data.value: Vermiculite
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InVermiculiteDoes
data.value: Holds several times its weight in water. Packs down if pressed hard.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InCastings
data.value: Worm castings
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InCastingsDoes
data.value: A gentle feed that also holds water.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InCharcoal
data.value: Charcoal
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InCharcoalDoes
data.value: Drainage.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_InSphagnumMoss
data.value: Sphagnum moss
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of an ingredient.

data.name: Mix_InSphagnumMossDoes
data.value: Holds a lot of water. Used on top for plants that like it damp.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: what the ingredient does.

data.name: Mix_Starts
data.value: Starting points
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: label over the choice of plants.

data.name: Mix_StartsNote
data.value: Each is a starting point to change to suit the plant and how you water, not a fixed recipe.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: line under the label over the choice of plants.

data.name: Mix_Foliage
data.value: Most foliage plants
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of a group of plants.

data.name: Mix_Aroids
data.value: Aroids
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of a group of plants.

data.name: Mix_AroidsNote
data.value: monstera, philodendron, anthurium
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: examples under Aroids.

data.name: Mix_Cacti
data.value: Cacti and succulents
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of a group of plants.

data.name: Mix_Orchids
data.value: Orchids
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: name of a group of plants.

data.name: Mix_Foliage1
data.value: 2 parts peat or coir, 1 part perlite, 1 part coarse sand.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Foliage2
data.value: Or 1 part peat or coir, 1 part bark, 1 part coarse sand.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Aroids1
data.value: A chunky mix for thick roots: coir with perlite, bark and pumice, and some worm castings and charcoal.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Aroids2
data.value: Many growers use a simpler one: about half multipurpose compost, with bark and perlite making up the rest.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Cacti1
data.value: Loam-based compost with up to 30 percent grit or fine gravel, or a ready-made cactus compost.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Cacti2
data.value: Or 2 parts soil, 1 part peat or coir, 1 part perlite, 1 part coarse sand.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_Orchids1
data.value: Mostly bark. Specialist orchid mixes are sold ready to use.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: a starting point.

data.name: Mix_InApp
data.value: Save a mix you like on Soil mixes, in parts, so you can pick it when you repot.
data.comment: Guide, mixing soil: how it works in the app. Uses the name of the Soil mixes page.
